title: When Your Ex-Girlfriend Turns You Crazy
description:
Submit a tip! Tips@Midwest-Safety.com

Please consider JOINING for $1 a month. It *really* helps us do original reporting like this. 

CONTACT US:
Complaints? Video submissions? Sponsorships? Collabs? Business inquires? 
Email our board at mn.safety.alerts@gmail.com. 

BE NICE:
The individuals presented in these videos may be suffering from the effects of alcohol, drug abuse, a mental health disorder or simply having a bad day. The videos should NOT be presumed to be representative of their general behavior. Everyone deserves to be treated with respect. 

RIGHT TO BE FORGOTTEN:
Midwest Safety practices the "Right to be Forgotten." If you were the suspect in a lower-level offense, you may email our board to request removal. 
Email: mn.safety.alerts@gmail.com

Surveillance footage reveals that after the male allegedly attempted to run over his girlfriend with his car, he left the scene while his girlfriend walked away. Reports indicate that prior to this incident, the male suspect had thrown a brick at his girlfriend for an undisclosed reason. The suspect, identified as Anthony, was charged with second degree recklessly endangering safety, possession of cocaine, his second and subsequent offense of possession of narcotic drugs. Fleeing, eluding. Fleeing, eluding, causing bodily harm or property damage. Three counts of felony bail jumping, misdemeanor bail jumping, resisting obstructing, and hit and run. Anthony pleaded guilty to possession of cocaine, fleeing, eluding. Fleeing eluding causing bodily harm or property damage. One count of felony bail jumping and hit and run. The rest of the charges were dismissed. Anthony was ultimately sentenced to three years in prison, three years of extended supervision, and a driver's license suspension for one year. However, he was given 671 days of jail credit, meaning he will serve only one year and 59 days in prison. This isn't just a traffic stop or a chase, it's a domestic understress, and those don't de-escalate on their own. They either get managed or they explode. Domestics don't always blow up loud and fast. Sometimes they slowly escalate because people lose control and they can't self-regulate and they feel like they don't have options. And once someone runs, they've already decided they're done talking. And this guy fled twice and that isn't fear, it's refusal, refusal to face the situation and refusal to slow the moment down while he could. And when police showed up, they didn't act impulsively. They gave him space, they gave him time, they gave him every chance to talk. But he chose to run over using his words. Then comes to detail you can't ignore or soften, because when someone puts a canine in a headlock, that's not resistance. That's lethal intent, and in my opinion, he knew exactly what he was going. If he was willing to choke a dog to avoid consequences, who do you think might have been next if this guy got away? But here's a lesson that you learned after enough years as a cop. Calls are not as they initially appear. Because it looks like emotion is usually covering fear, guilt, or something illegal on someone or in the car. Remember, cops don't always get the whole story when they receive the call. They find out as the situation is unfolding and sometimes it gets uglier by the second. And once someone decides control matters more than stopping, hesitation stops. being restraint and becomes more of a risk.
